"So the doctor says Abbu's heart is 'a bit dramatic'," Wasim said, grinning. "Runs in the family."
Lalremsiami laughed. "At least he's consistent."
"And the hospital canteen samosas could kill a healthy man. We're doing great."
She laughed again, then stopped. "Wasim, that's the fourth joke about the hospital today."
"What, I'm funny."
"You are. It's helping, I can tell. But you haven't said one serious thing since Monday."
Wasim looked at his tea. The grin stayed a second too long, then slipped.
"If I stop joking," he said quietly, "I think I'll fall apart in the middle of class."
"Then fall apart here. I've got time."
He talked for half an hour: the scans, his mother not sleeping, his fear of the surgery.
"Should I tell the class advisor?" he asked finally.
"Let's go together, now. She can give you leave for the surgery week."

qa.a: The fourth joke about the hospital today.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling underneath the jokes?
qa.a: He was frightened and overwhelmed about his father's surgery, and afraid he would fall apart; the jokes were helping him cope.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do that helped?
qa.a: She laughed with him but noticed the constant joking, made room for a serious talk, and went with him to the class advisor that day.

qa.q: What would change if Lalremsiami had just kept laughing along?
qa.a: Wasim might have kept hiding his fear behind jokes and missed support like leave for the surgery week.

grounding: Shows a young adult using humour to cope with stress and a friend noticing that constant joking may hide distress needing a serious talk.

passage: I remember our final-year exam month mostly as laughter. I'm Indu, and Rashmi was my study partner. When we were stuck on accounts at midnight, she'd do impressions of our professor, and I'd laugh till my stomach hurt. It really helped; we'd go back to the problems lighter. But around the third week, I noticed her jokes had changed. They were darker. "If I fail, I'll just become a professional samosa taster." "Nobody would notice if I disappeared from the batch anyway." Everyone laughed. I didn't, the second time. That night, after the others left, I asked, "Rashmi, are you okay? Not joke-okay. Real okay." She was quiet for a long time, then cried and said she hadn't slept properly in two weeks and felt hopeless. I stayed with her, and we called the college counsellor's night helpline together, right then. The counsellor talked to her for forty minutes and fixed a meeting for the morning. I walked her there myself.

qa.a: She did impressions of their professor.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling beneath the darker jokes?
qa.a: She was exhausted and hopeless, not having slept properly in two weeks, and the jokes were covering that distress.

qa.q: What did Indu do that was right when the jokes turned dark?
qa.a: Indu stopped laughing, asked privately if Rashmi was really okay, stayed with her, and called the counsellor's helpline with her that same night.

qa.q: How did the others in the group seem to hear Rashmi's darker jokes?
qa.a: They laughed, likely taking them as ordinary exam humour and missing the distress underneath.

grounding: Shows humour easing exam stress and bonding friends, and a friend noticing when constant dark joking hides distress that needs serious, same-night help.

passage:
Supervisor's note, software team, Wednesday.
Our release failed badly last night; the site was down for two hours. This morning Tanvir, the junior who pushed the update, walked in and announced, "Good news, everyone: I've discovered a new way to break production." The team laughed, and the mood in the room eased. Humour like that can help a team get through a hard morning, and I didn't want to shut it down. But I noticed Tanvir kept joking all through the review, even when we were looking at the error logs, and his hands were shaking on the keyboard. At lunch I asked him to walk with me. I said I liked his humour but wanted to check how he was really feeling. He said he'd been awake all night, sure he'd be fired. I told him clearly that he won't be, that we'd fix the process together, and that he could talk to me or the staff counsellor anytime. He looked relieved. I'll check again on Friday.
— Parul

qa.a: For two hours.

qa.a: They laughed and the mood in the room eased, so the humour helped the whole team through a hard morning.

grounding: Shows a young adult using jokes to cope after a failure, and a supervisor noticing when constant joking hides distress.

passage: At the primary health centre in Barsana, Devika worked at the reception desk. That afternoon the doctor handed her a note for Lalit, who was waiting for his mother's test results. The doctor had written: "Sugar high. Must see me tomorrow, 9 a.m." Devika didn't want to scare him. "Your mother's results are... a little unusual," she said gently. "Nothing to worry about too much." Lalit smiled with relief and got up to leave. "So we can skip coming back?" Devika's stomach dropped. Her softness had blurred the one thing that mattered. "Wait, Lalit. I said that badly. The doctor needs to see your mother tomorrow at nine. Her sugar is high. It's important not to miss it." Lalit sat down again, serious now. "Okay. Nine. I'll bring her." Devika wrote the time on a slip for him, clearly, in big numbers.

qa.a: Her soft wording made the result sound unimportant; she corrected herself with a clear message about the time and why it mattered, and wrote it down.

qa.a: He took it as good news and felt relieved, thinking they could skip coming back.

grounding: Shows a young adult using a soft euphemism to spare feelings and realising that in health matters clarity must come first.

passage: At a friend's birthday dinner in Kraków, someone asked Layla what she was doing these days. Layla had been let go from her marketing job three weeks earlier. "Oh, I'm between jobs," she said lightly, and changed the subject to the cake. Everyone nodded. Later, walking to the tram, her friend Marek asked, "Between jobs as in taking a break, or...?" Layla hesitated. With the table, the soft phrase had been right; nobody needed the details. But Marek had offered last month to pass her CV to his company. "Honestly? I was let go. Budget cuts. I didn't want to say it in front of everyone." Marek nodded. "That's fair. I'm glad you told me, though. I'll send your CV tomorrow." Layla felt her shoulders loosen. passage: In the college chemistry lab, Aditi, a final-year student helping the juniors, showed Kalyani around on her first day. At the gas cylinder in the corner, Aditi said, "This one's a bit temperamental. Just be gentle with it." Kalyani nodded, smiling. An hour later, Aditi smelled gas. Kalyani was standing at the cylinder, twisting the valve hard. Aditi rushed over, shut it, opened the windows and called the lab assistant. Nobody was hurt. Afterwards her hands were shaking. She sat Kalyani down. "That was my fault. 'Temperamental' was the wrong word. What I meant: the valve leaks if you force it. Never open it without Ramesh sir checking the seal first. If you smell gas, leave and tell him." Kalyani nodded, pale. "I thought 'temperamental' meant slow." Aditi wrote the rule on a card and taped it to the cylinder that same afternoon.

qa.q: Who should check the seal before the cylinder is opened?
qa.a: Ramesh sir.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling after the gas incident?
qa.a: She was shaken and guilty, her hands shaking, and took the blame for her vague word.

qa.q: What did Aditi do to make the safety message clear?
qa.a: She explained plainly what the valve does, gave exact rules about checking and leaving if there's a smell, and taped the rule to the cylinder.

qa.q: How did Kalyani understand the word "temperamental"?
qa.a: She took it to mean slow, so she twisted the valve hard, not realising it was a warning about leaks.

grounding: Shows a young adult realising a soft, tactful word blurred a safety message and replacing it with clear instructions.

passage: I'm Sahil, and I went with Aparna to the student art show on the last day of term. She stopped in front of a big canvas: a white dove above a lit clay lamp, on a red background. "Peace and hope," she said at once. "Dove is peace, lamp is hope." A girl standing nearby, whose name tag said Mariam, smiled. "Maybe. For me, a dove is the Holy Spirit. My church uses it." Then an older visitor added that in his village red was for weddings, not war. Aparna frowned, then laughed. "So I've just read it through my own eyes." She walked closer and found the artist's note on the wall: the painting was about the artist's grandmother's funeral. Aparna stood there a long time. I don't know what she felt, but she was quiet all the way to the canteen, and then said, "I'll ask before I decide next time."

qa.q: What did the artist's note say the painting was about?
qa.a: The artist's grandmother's funeral.

qa.q: What might Aparna have been feeling as she stood reading the artist's note?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and thoughtful, perhaps a little humbled, since her confident reading of peace and hope missed the painting's grief.

qa.q: What did Aparna decide to do differently?
qa.a: To ask or look for context before deciding what a symbol means.

qa.q: How did Mariam's reading of the dove differ from Aparna's?
qa.a: For Mariam the dove meant the Holy Spirit from her church, while Aparna read it as peace.

grounding: Shows through an observer a young adult learning that symbols like a dove, a lamp and colours carry different meanings across cultures and faiths.

passage: Manjula, you're asking what the lamp at your friend's door means. Let your Anjali aunty tell you what happened when I was twenty. I visited my college friend Mercy's home in Kottayam for the first time. There was a small oil lamp burning in front of a picture of Mother Mary. I folded my hands, the way I would before our lamp at home, and asked, "Is it for Diwali?" Mercy's grandmother laughed kindly. "No, mole. For us, it's for the prayers, and for my husband, who died on this day." I felt so silly. I had seen a lamp and thought I knew everything. Then she let me light a second wick with her. I think of it every Diwali now. A lamp in my house means welcome and light. In hers, it meant prayer and remembering. Ask, beta. Don't assume.

Warden's note, girls' hostel, results day.
When the final-year results came out, most of the girls ran to phone their families. Hafsa, who had topped her department, did something I hadn't seen before in our hostel. She went quietly to the prayer corner in the common room, knelt and bowed her forehead to the floor for a few moments, then sat still with her eyes closed. A couple of first-years stared and giggled. Nilesh, our hostel caretaker's son who helps with maintenance, was fixing the fan and stopped working until she had finished. Afterwards I asked Hafsa, gently, what it meant. She said it was a prostration of thanks, and that before celebrating anything she thanks God first. I told the first-years later that people give thanks in many ways, and that this was hers. I think Hafsa's quiet moment meant more to her than the loud calls meant to the others.
— Mrs Lobo

Karthik came home with me for Nabanna, the harvest festival in my Dida's village near Bardhaman. I'm Asif, and even though we're Muslim, our village celebrates the new rice together; everyone brings something. This morning Dida made the first rice of the season with jaggery and milk and set a plate aside before anyone ate. "The first share is thanks for the harvest," she said. Karthik looked confused. "Is that a prayer?" I wasn't sure how to explain. For Dida it's thanks to God, for the neighbours it's thanks to the earth and the gods, and for me it's thanks for Abbu's field doing well this year after two bad ones. Karthik said, "In Tamil Nadu we have Pongal. We let the milk boil over for plenty." We both went quiet when Dida lit the lamp. It felt like the same thanks in different clothes.
— Asif

Sunday, after the engagement lunch.
Karthik met my whole family today in Kolkata. When my Dida and Dadu came in, all my cousins did pranam, touching their feet, and so did I. I'd warned Karthik it might happen and told him he didn't have to. His family does namaskaram at home, but only for their own elders, and he said he'd feel strange doing it on the first day with people he'd just met.
He chose to fold his hands and bow low instead. Dadu looked surprised for a second. Then Dida said, loudly, "What a respectful boy!" and everyone laughed.
Later my Mashi whispered that some relatives might have expected pranam. Maybe. But Karthik looked at ease, and Dida clearly liked him. I'd rather he chose what felt real. Next Durga Puja, if he wants to, he can.
— Sonali

passage:
Class teacher's note, first-year economics, Monday.
Kamal, a Deaf student, joined our section this term with a sign language interpreter, Ms Farida. In the first week I noticed two problems. When classmates asked Kamal questions, they looked at Ms Farida and said, "Ask him if he has notes." Kamal's face showed he'd noticed. Also, in discussions, people kept talking over each other, and Ms Farida couldn't keep up; Kamal often raised his hand just after the topic had moved on. Today I gave the class two simple rules: speak directly to Kamal, not to the interpreter, and pause a few seconds after a question so the interpretation can catch up. We also turned on captions for videos. In this afternoon's discussion, Irawati asked Kamal directly for his view, then waited. He answered through Ms Farida, and the class actually heard him. I'll check with Kamal next week about what else would help.
— Mr Sen

qa.q: What did Mr Sen turn on for videos?
qa.a: Captions.

qa.q: What might Kamal have been feeling when classmates spoke to the interpreter about him?
qa.a: His face showed he'd noticed, suggesting he felt left out and talked about rather than to.

qa.q: What changes did Mr Sen make, and why do they help?
qa.a: Speaking directly to Kamal, pausing for the interpreter's lag and using captions, so Kamal could join discussions on time.

qa.q: How did Irawati include Kamal in the afternoon discussion?
qa.a: She asked Kamal directly for his view and then waited, so his answer came through before the topic moved on.

grounding: Shows a classroom learning to speak directly to a Deaf student and wait for the interpreter's lag, supported by captions.

Thursday.
Group project meeting with Santosh today. Santosh is Deaf, and his interpreter, Mrs Rao, came with him. I'm Harsha, and I realised halfway through that I'd been talking to Mrs Rao the whole time, saying things like "Can he do the survey part?" Santosh was sitting right there. He tapped the table and signed, and Mrs Rao said, "I'm right here, Harsha. Ask me." My face burned.
After that I turned to Santosh and asked him directly. I also noticed the gap: Mrs Rao needs a few seconds to interpret. Whenever I asked a question and jumped in again too fast, Santosh missed the chance to answer. So I counted three in my head each time. It felt slow at first, then normal.
By the end, Santosh had taken the survey section and suggested a better sample. Next time I'll send the agenda the night before so he can prepare too.
— Harsha

passage: At the community centre's Saturday Deaf club, Abhinav, three weeks into learning sign language, watched Eshaan tell a story about a near accident on his scooter. Abhinav fixed his eyes on Eshaan's hands, trying to catch each sign. He was lost within seconds. The teacher, Mrs Iyer, leaned over and whispered, "Don't just watch the hands. Watch the whole space." Abhinav looked again. Eshaan had set something on his left and something on his right. His flat hand moved from the left like a vehicle, fast, then swerved. His other hand, shaped differently, stood for the scooter. His face tightened, eyes wide, as the two hands almost met. Suddenly Abhinav could see it: a car came from the left, cut across, and Eshaan swerved. Abhinav laughed out loud with relief. Eshaan grinned at him and signed something with raised eyebrows, which Mrs Iyer said was a question: "You got it?"

qa.q: Where did Eshaan set things while telling the story?
qa.a: On his left and on his right.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he finally understood the story?
qa.a: He felt relief and delight, laughing out loud after being lost at first.

qa.a: Mrs Iyer's advice to watch the whole signing space, not just the hands.

Dear Seema,
Thank you for Friday. I've been thinking about it all weekend.
You know I've been learning sign for two months. I thought I was doing well, collecting signs like words in a notebook. Then at lunch you told the story of your nephew's cricket match, and I understood almost nothing, even though I knew many of the signs.
What I missed, I realise now, was the space. You put the batsman in one place and the bowler in another, then just pointed back instead of repeating them. Your hand became the ball and flew across. Your face showed the crowd's shock. It wasn't a list of signs. It was a whole scene you built in the air.
When you retold it slowly and I watched the space instead of your fingers, I got it, and laughed at the ending.
Can we have lunch again Friday?
Noor

qa.a: Seema's nephew's cricket match.

passage: You're asking what it's like watching my cousin Tarun sign, for your podcast? I'm Charu. Tarun's Deaf, and I grew up signing with him, but friends who are learning always ask how I follow him so fast. Here's the thing. They watch his hands like they're reading words one by one. I watch everything at once. When Tarun tells me about his fight with his landlord, he puts the landlord on his right, himself on his left, and after that he just turns his body or points to show who's talking. When he talks about his bike weaving through traffic, one hand becomes the bike and the other the cars, and I can see the whole road. His eyebrows, his mouth, the speed of his hands, all of it is grammar. My friend Anu once told me she'd understood 'landlord' and 'angry' and nothing else. I told her to stop reading his fingers and start watching the whole story.

qa.q: Where does Tarun place the landlord when he signs?
qa.a: On his right.

qa.q: What was Anu likely feeling when she understood only two signs?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated and confused, having caught only 'landlord' and 'angry' while trying to read each sign.

qa.q: What advice does Charu give learners?
qa.a: Stop reading his fingers one by one and watch the whole signing space, including the face and the speed.

qa.q: How does Charu see the way learners watch Tarun?
qa.a: Charu sees them reading his hands like single words, missing the space and face that carry the meaning.

grounding: Shows a young adult explaining how signers use space and hand shapes for people and objects, and that watching the whole space gives meaning.

passage: I'm Mehak, and I was in the library with Kashish when she wrote to Professor Rao about her missed deadline. She typed: "hey sir, cant submit today, can u extend pls? thx." I leaned over and read it. "You're sending that to Rao sir?" Kashish shrugged. "It's short. He's busy." I said nothing, but I could picture Rao sir's eyebrows. She hesitated, then deleted it. She wrote again, slowly: "Dear Professor Rao, I'm writing to ask whether I might submit my assignment on Friday instead of today. My grandmother was admitted to hospital last night. I'm sorry for the inconvenience and will send it by Friday noon. Thank you for considering this. Regards, Kashish Arora, 2nd year B.Com." Then she texted her friend Priya: "grandma in hospital 😔 sir might kill me lol." Same afternoon, two completely different voices. Rao sir replied in an hour: "Of course. Hope she recovers soon."

qa.q: When did Kashish ask to submit the assignment instead?
qa.a: On Friday instead of today.

qa.q: What might Kashish have been feeling as she rewrote the email?
qa.a: She seemed hesitant and worried about how the professor would react, especially with her grandmother in hospital.

qa.q: What did Kashish change in the second email, and why did it work?
qa.a: She used a formal greeting, full sentences, a reason, an apology, a clear date and a sign-off, which showed respect and got a quick, kind reply.

qa.q: How might Professor Rao have read the first draft?
qa.a: He might have found it too casual and disrespectful, with "hey sir" and "pls", and been less willing to help.

grounding: Shows a young adult adjusting the register of an email from casual to formal for a professor, while keeping an informal voice with a friend.

passage:
Monday. Pooja got a job interview invitation and replied: "Hi!! Thanks so much, sounds awesome, see u Thurs 😊". Her flatmate Jahnavi read it over her shoulder and winced. "Pooja, that's a bank."

passage: Binita, since you're writing to your first boss, let your Arnab mama tell you about my first letter to mine. I was twenty-one and had just joined a tea estate office in Jorhat. I needed two days' leave for my sister's wedding. I wrote to the manager, Mr Barua, the way I'd write to my college friends: "Barua da, need 2 days off next week, sister's wedding. Hope OK. Arnab." He called me in and held up the note. "Da? Hope OK?" My ears went red. He wasn't angry, just firm. "Here we write: 'Respected Sir, I request leave for two days, the 10th and 11th, for my sister's wedding. I will complete the accounts before I go.' You see? Same message. But now I know you respect the office." I rewrote it at his table. He signed it and even sent a gift for the wedding. I still write that way to seniors.

qa.q: Why did young Arnab need two days' leave?
qa.a: For his sister's wedding.

qa.q: How did young Arnab feel when Mr Barua held up the note?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his ears going red, realising his casual note didn't suit the office.

qa.q: What turning point in the story taught Arnab about register?
qa.a: Mr Barua firmly showed him how to write the same request formally, and Arnab rewrote it at his table.

qa.q: How did Mr Barua see the casual note?
qa.a: He saw it as too informal for the office, though he wasn't angry, and wanted Arnab to show respect in writing.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to adjust written register to a senior, with greeting, courtesy and detail that signal respect.

passage: In a Copenhagen café, Anders pushed his laptop across the table to Selin. "My personal statement for the master's. Tell me it's brilliant." Selin read: "I am a passionate, hard-working team player who has always loved the environment and wants to make the world a better place." She looked up. "Anders, this could be anyone." He groaned. "It's supposed to sound impressive." "What did you actually do last summer?" "I counted bicycles at six crossings for the city, for eight weeks, in the rain. And I found that two crossings had far more near-misses than the others, and the city put in new lights." Selin smiled. "Write that." He rewrote the opening: "Last summer I spent eight weeks counting bicycles at six Copenhagen crossings, in the rain." It read like a real person. Selin said, "Leave out the rain complaints, though. Nobody needs your whole self in one page."

qa.q: How many crossings did Anders count bicycles at?
qa.a: Six crossings.

qa.q: What was Anders feeling when Selin said "this could be anyone"?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and deflated, groaning, since he'd tried to sound impressive.

qa.q: What made Anders's rewritten opening stronger?
qa.a: It used honest, specific detail about what he actually did and found, instead of generic claims.

qa.q: What does Selin mean by "Nobody needs your whole self in one page"?
qa.a: She means a personal statement is a chosen, curated picture, so he should keep the relevant details and leave out the rest.

grounding: Shows a young adult replacing generic claims with honest, specific detail in a personal statement that is a curated self-presentation.

passage: In the university career centre, Chaitanya handed his job-portal profile to the counsellor, Disha. "Results-driven go-getter with excellent communication skills and a passion for innovation." Disha read it twice. "What results? What did you drive?" Chaitanya laughed nervously. "I don't know. Everyone writes this." "Tell me one thing you did that you're proud of." He thought. "I ran the canteen's food waste survey. We cut waste by a third in two months by changing portion sizes." Disha tapped the table. "That's your first line." They worked through it: the survey, the teaching he did for his cousins during lockdown, the time he fixed the department's booking sheet. She stopped him when he added that he had 'no weaknesses'. "Don't claim you're perfect. Show what you've done." Chaitanya read the final version. "It sounds like me," he said, surprised. "The good parts of you," Disha said. "That's what a profile is."

qa.q: By how much did the canteen survey cut food waste?
qa.a: By a third in two months.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when Disha asked what results he drove?
qa.a: He felt nervous and a bit embarrassed, laughing and admitting he'd written what everyone writes.

qa.q: How did Disha help Chaitanya improve his profile?
qa.a: She asked for a real achievement, helped him build the profile from specific examples, and stopped him from claiming he had no weaknesses.

qa.q: How does Disha see what a profile is?
qa.a: As a curated picture of "the good parts" of a person, not the whole self.

grounding: Shows a young adult replacing generic claims with honest, specific details in a profile, which is a curated self-presentation.

Dear Deepika,
You asked me to read your statement for the fellowship, and I will. But first, a confession about mine, because I think it'll help.
My first draft said I was "deeply committed to social change since childhood". Honestly? Since childhood I was committed to cricket. What changed was one summer, when I volunteered at the night school in our basti and a boy of fifteen asked me to help him read his ration card. That's the true start.
So I wrote that instead. It felt risky, less shiny. But the interviewer brought it up first and asked about him.
I also left out a lot: my failed first year, my messy family stuff. That's not lying, I think; the statement is the part of me that fits this door, not the whole house.
So for yours: what's your ration-card moment?
Abhinav

passage:
Wednesday night.
Sent Tanvir a long message this afternoon about changing our trip dates, with three options and a joke. The reply came an hour later: "k."
Just "k." With a full stop.
My stomach knotted. Is Tanvir angry? Last week I cancelled on the movie. Maybe this is payback. I typed three long replies and deleted all of them. I couldn't focus on my assignment.
At nine I just called. Tanvir picked up, sounding cheerful. "Hey! Sorry, I was in the lab all day, typing with gloves on. 'k' meant okay, option two is perfect." I laughed from relief. I told Tanvir about my three deleted replies and we both laughed more.
Note to self: a short message is usually a busy person, not an angry one. And a call takes thirty seconds.
— Nitin

qa.q: What was Tanvir's reply?
What was Nitin feeling after reading "k."?
qa.a: Nitin felt anxious and unsettled, stomach knotted, worrying Tanvir was angry about the cancelled movie.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that cleared things up?
qa.a: Nitin called instead of guessing, which quickly showed the reply was just rushed.

qa.q: Why was Tanvir's reply so short?
qa.a: Tanvir had been in the lab all day typing with gloves on, so "k" simply meant okay, option two.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading a short text as anger and learning, through a call, that it was just rushed.

passage: Rukmini had worked at the panchayat office in Kallur for only two weeks when her phone buzzed at seven in the morning. It was from Lokesh, the secretary. "Come to office. Now." Her heart raced. Had she made a mistake in the ration lists? She hadn't even had tea. She walked fast through the lanes, rehearsing apologies. At the office she found Lokesh on the phone, shouting over a bad line, surrounded by files. He waved her in, covered the phone and said, "Thank god. The district officer is coming at nine, and you're the only one who knows the new computer system. Can you print the lists?" Rukmini let out a long breath. "I thought I was in trouble!" Lokesh looked puzzled. "Why?" She showed him the message. He laughed. "I typed with one thumb while the officer was on the other line. Sorry. Next time I'll add 'please'."

qa.q: What time did the district officer plan to come?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she read "Come to office. Now."?
qa.a: She was anxious and scared, her heart racing, sure she had made a mistake in the ration lists.

qa.q: What could Rukmini try next time a message seems harsh?
qa.a: Call or reply with a quick clarifying question before assuming she is in trouble, since short messages are often just rushed.

qa.q: How did Lokesh see his own message?
qa.a: He saw it as a rushed note typed with one thumb during a call, and didn't realise it sounded harsh until Rukmini showed him.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading a brief text as anger when it was only rushed, and the value of checking.
